title: The Copy That Lags

post.author: u/westerby_registrar_ilsabet
post.title: I'm the night registrar at our town's new hall. A couple married at 23:58 are in the old hall's book and not in ours, and both halls have given record No. 4471 to different people.

blocks.text: Our town sits on both banks of the river. The old hall in Osterby has kept the register, the official record of births, deaths and marriages, since 1874. Each new entry gets the next record number. It keeps a night register, so people can come at any hour. I work nights at the new hall in Westerby, which holds a copy. Every entry the old hall makes goes into its log, the running list of every change in order, like a ship's logbook. The log goes out on the old hall's one line out, the cable to the copies, entry after entry. It goes to two copies: the annex, a records room across the square, and us, under the bridge. Our copy is usually about two seconds behind.

Last spring the council's contractor, Mr Threlfall, put a watchdog in our hall: a program that keeps watch on the old hall. It works in steps. It listens to the old hall's line. If the old hall says nothing for five minutes, it decides the old hall is gone. Then it makes our copy the register, taking new entries itself.

On Saturday at 23:57:30 Absalom Kerridge, the old hall's night clerk, filed the scans of the 1911 register, pictures of 600 pages. At 23:58:12 Cordelia Lusk and Tancred Bramwell were married at the old hall's counter as No. 4471, and walked out with their certificate, the paper that proves it. At 23:59:00 the old hall went dark. In Mr Threlfall's log below, each line shows the time, which hall or program wrote it, and what happened: an entry and its number, the state of the line, or how far our copy was behind (s means seconds):

23:57:30  old hall   scans, 1911 book, 600 pages   line out busy until 23:59:30
23:58:12  old hall   No. 4471  MARRIAGE  LUSK / BRAMWELL   certificate printed
23:58:41  old hall   No. 4472  BIRTH   certificate printed
23:58:42  new hall   notice board: No. 4471 NOT FOUND
23:59:00  old hall   DARK   new hall copy: last No. 4470, 90 s behind
00:04:00  watchdog   5 min of silence   new hall is the register   next No. 4471
00:31:00  new hall   No. 4471  DEATH   certificate printed
05:47:00  old hall   back
At 05:52 the old hall's day clerk, who hadn't been told, registered a birth as No. 4473. We had given 4473 to a death at 02:40.
In the old hall's book, 4471 is a wedding. In ours, 4471 is a death.

At eight Mrs Lusk came to my counter with her certificate, to ask for a copy of it. Our book has never heard of her. Neither has the annex's. Mr Threlfall says the copies are only ever seconds behind. There's a brass plate by the old hall's counter that I'd never properly read until this morning:

blocks.title: NOTICE
items: UNTIL THE CLERK ACROSS THE SQUARE HAS WRITTEN THE ENTRY IN HIS BOOK.

blocks.text: What should we change before next Saturday?

blocks.label: threlfall_dashboard_saturday.png

diagram.aria: Mr Threlfall's dashboard for Saturday from 23:57:00 to 00:05:00. The old hall is up until 23:59:00, then dark. Its line out is idle until 23:57:30, then busy with the scans until the old hall goes dark. The annex follows the old hall until 23:59:00, gets nothing until 00:04:00, then follows the new hall. The new hall's copy falls behind from 23:57:30 and becomes the register at 00:04:00. Markers: scans at 23:57:30, No. 4471 at 23:58:12, dark at 23:59:00, promoted at 00:04:00.

blocks.caption: Mr Threlfall's dashboard for Saturday night. From 23:57:30 the old hall's line out was busy with the 600 pages of scans, 120 s of them. No. 4471 was married at 23:58:12. When the old hall went dark at 23:59:00, our copy's last entry was No. 4470 and we were 90 s behind. At 00:04:00 the watchdog made us the register, and the annex started following us.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your halls run leader and followers. One copy, the leader, takes every write, every new entry. The others, the followers, keep copies. It works in steps. The leader writes the entry into its log. It sends the log down the line. Each follower replays it, entry by entry, in the same order. You met that log in the ship's engine room, and a copy that lags behind in the library's back room. What matters tonight is when the leader says done, here by printing the certificate. Saying done is called acknowledging, or confirming, the write. Asynchronous (async): at once, before any follower has the entry. Synchronous: only once every follower it names has it. Semi-synchronous (semi-sync): once at least one follower has it. Making a follower the new leader is called promoting it, and the switch is a failover. Fencing is making sure the old leader can't take writes any more, even if it wakes up, for example by locking its book so it can only be read. Now your log. What was the line out carrying from 23:57:30 to 23:59:00, and where in that queue was No. 4471? When did the couple get their certificate, and what had reached either copy by then? What did the watchdog know at 00:04? And at 05:47, what did the old hall think it was?

replies.author: u/westerby_registrar_ilsabet
replies.text: Mr Threlfall says the line out sends one entry at a time, in order, and nothing goes until the one before it has gone; the scans took it two minutes. His dashboard, his screen of live numbers, shows our lag, how far behind we were, over the hour before as p50 2.2 s and p99 6.3 s, and the annex's as 0.2 s and 0.4 s. He says p50 means half the entries reached us within 2.2 s; you can read p99 the same way. There were 20 registrations that hour, one every 3 minutes. The rest of Saturday night: a death at my counter at 00:31; a birth at the old hall at 01:15, who found it dark and crossed the bridge, ten minutes, so ours at 01:25 as 4472; a death here at 02:40, 4473; a birth at 04:05 who crossed too, 4474 at 04:15; a death here at 05:20, 4475. Our notice board reads each old-hall entry from our own copy 30 seconds after it's made, and Mr Threlfall calls a miss there a stale read. He says somebody will have to reconcile the two books by hand: go through them entry by entry and decide what to keep.

comments.author: u/seconds_not_minutes_dagobert
comments.text: Five minutes is your bug. For five minutes of silence nobody in your town can register anything, and people at a counter at midnight don't wait. The lesson from every outage I've worked: fail over in seconds, not minutes. Our payments database promotes its standby, the follower kept ready to take over, automatically after 10 seconds of silence, no human in the loop, and nobody even notices. Set the watchdog to 10 seconds and the new hall is the register at 23:59:10.

comments.author: u/both_books_gwenllian
comments.text: Your brass plate already says it, and it's what synchronous replication is for: no certificate until every copy has written the entry, so nothing a clerk has confirmed can ever be missing from a copy. It works in steps. The leader writes the entry. It sends it to every copy. It waits until each copy says it has written it. Only then does it print the certificate. Our bank runs PostgreSQL, the database program from the library case. Each commit, the moment a change is made to count, waits for the standbys named in a setting, synchronous_standby_names. Ours lists both standbys with FIRST 2, so it waits for both. Make both your copies synchronous and No. 4471 is in every book or in none.

comments.author: u/wait_for_daylight_torvald
comments.text: Honestly, take the watchdog out. A program can't tell a dark hall from a cut line; both look like silence. If the old hall goes dark, phone the superintendent registrar, the person in charge of the register, and let a person decide, with light to see by. You'll never have two books again. You'll also have people standing at a locked door.

reply.prompt: Next Saturday Absalom files the scans at 23:57:30 again, and another couple will be at the old hall's counter at 23:58:12. What should the halls change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Set the watchdog to promote the new hall after 10 seconds of silence, so the town is never long without a register.
options.part2: Mr Threlfall set the watchdog to 10 seconds. On Saturday Absalom filed the scans at 23:57:30 again, and at 23:58:12 a couple were married as No. 4471 and left with their certificate. At 23:59:00 the line under the bridge dropped for 43 seconds. The old hall stayed lit. At 23:59:10 the watchdog heard 10 seconds of silence and made us the register, lacking the scans, No. 4471 and No. 4472, all three confirmed. At 23:59:43 the line came back, and the old hall carried on registering too: two registers, all night. By morning 4471, 4472 and 4473 each had two owners, and our notice board had missed 5 of the old hall's entries. The wedding was, again, in their book and not in ours. Dagobert was right about one thing: nobody noticed until morning.
options.senior: A faster failover shortens the outage, but it can't change what the follower has. The 3 entries were still queued on the line out at 23:59:00, so they are lost at 10 seconds exactly as at 5 minutes. And a short timeout can't tell a dead leader from a 43-second blip: promoting during a blip gives you two leaders taking writes at once. In October 2018 GitHub, the code-sharing site, lost a line for 43 seconds: this night at continental scale. Automatic failover needs fencing, and no failover brings back a write that never left.

options.text: Make both copies synchronous: no certificate until the annex and the new hall have each written the entry in their book.
options.verdict: Safe until a copy goes dark
options.part2: Mr Threlfall made both copies synchronous. Every certificate now waits for the slower copy, us: 2.2 seconds at the median, p50, and 6.3 at p99, where before it was none. On Saturday the scans at 23:57:30 and the marriage at 23:58:12 both waited for the line, and when the old hall went dark at 23:59:00 none of the three had been confirmed, so nothing acknowledged was lost. But at 00:04:00, when we became the register, every new entry had to wait for both other halls, and one of them was dark. The couple who came over the bridge at 00:09:00 were turned away, and so was everyone after them: 8 people by morning, the last at the old hall's own door at 05:52. No number was issued twice, because no number was issued.
options.senior: Sync to all makes every write as slow as the slowest follower, and with every follower required, one dead follower stops all writes. PostgreSQL's manual warns that such commits may never be completed if any one of the synchronous standbys should crash. Waiting for one of several followers, the nearest, keeps the guarantee that a confirmed write exists in two places without handing the leader's availability to its worst copy.

options.text: Take the watchdog out: when the old hall goes dark, wait for the registrar to come in and decide, however long it takes.
options.part2: Mr Threlfall took the watchdog out. On Saturday the old hall went dark at 23:59:00 with the scans, No. 4471 and No. 4472 still on the line, and nobody promoted us. The superintendent registrar came in, saw she couldn't tell what our copy was missing, and waited for the old hall. From 23:59 to 05:47 the town had no register: 5 people were turned away, 3 at my counter and 2 who crossed the bridge from the dark hall. At 05:47 the old hall came back as the register and sent us what we had missed. Nothing acknowledged was lost, and 4471 has one owner, the couple. The birth at 05:52 was No. 4473, once.
options.senior: Never failing over automatically means never losing a confirmed write to a failover and never having two leaders, which is why some teams choose it for their most precious data. The price is an outage as long as every repair: 5 hours 48 minutes here. A person who can't see what the follower lacks has no better choice than the watchdog's, only a slower one. Make sure a follower provably has every confirmed write, then let a machine promote it, with fencing.

options.text: No certificate until the annex has the entry, fence the old hall before the watchdog promotes, and reconcile by hand.
options.part2: Mr Threlfall set the old hall to print no certificate until one copy has the entry, which is always the annex, a fifth of a second away, and turned on fencing: before the watchdog promotes us, it locks the old hall's register, so the old hall comes back read-only: it can show its book but not add to it. In an ordinary hour, certificates now wait 0.2 seconds at the median and 0.4 at p99. On Saturday Absalom filed the scans at 23:57:30 again, and at 23:58:12 a couple stood at the old hall's counter as No. 4471. Their certificate didn't print: the entry was queued behind the scans, and no copy had it. At 23:59:00 the old hall went dark with the scans, No. 4471 and No. 4472 never confirmed. At 00:04:00 the watchdog fenced the old hall and promoted us, lacking no acknowledged write. At 00:09:00 the couple came over the bridge and were married at my counter as No. 4471, certificate after 2.2 seconds, and the birth became No. 4472. At 05:47 the old hall came back read-only, holding 3 entries we lacked, none of them confirmed and 2 registered again here. Absalom and I reconciled them by hand before breakfast, and he filed the scans again. Nothing acknowledged lost, no number issued twice, nobody turned away. Mrs Lusk says the brass plate was right all along.
options.senior: Asynchronous replication confirms a write before any follower has it, so a failover loses whatever was still on the line, here 3 entries, and nothing done to the failover itself changes that. Waiting for one nearby follower means every confirmed write exists in two places, for the price of one short round trip, there and back, 0.2 s here. A big write makes people wait behind it instead of vanishing. Fencing keeps the returning leader from taking writes, so there is one register. What it held but never confirmed still needs a person, because only a person can tell one marriage entered twice from two marriages.

sim.title: Run the twin halls' register
sim.lede: You're Mr Threlfall, replaying Saturday night from 23:57:20; the clock runs 30 times faster than real time, and Next event and Run to the end skip ahead. The old hall is the leader. Its log goes out on its one line out, one entry at a time, in order, to two followers: the annex has each entry 0.2 s after it is sent, the new hall 2.2 s after. Since 23:00 there have been 20 registrations, one every 3 minutes; over that hour the annex's lag was p50 0.2 s, p99 0.4 s, and the new hall's p50 2.2 s, p99 6.3 s. A fixed seed shuffles which registration got which lag, so those numbers never move, and from 23:57 the replay uses each copy's median. At 23:57:30 the scans hold the line out for 120 s. The rest of the night's registrations are the ones in OP's reply, and anyone who finds the old hall dark or locked crosses the bridge and reaches the new hall 10 minutes later. Pick the replication mode: async prints the certificate at once, semi-sync to one when the first copy has the entry (always the annex), sync to all when every other hall has it. A register that can't count on enough copies turns the registration away. Pick the failure (none, the old hall dark at 23:58:00 or at 23:59:00, or the line under the bridge down for 43 s while the old hall stays lit) and the failover: the watchdog in the new hall promotes it after 5 min or 10 s of silence, first copying anything it lacks from the annex if it can reach the annex, or nobody promotes and the registrar waits for the old hall. Fencing locks the old hall before promoting, so it comes back read-only. People whose certificate never printed cross to the new hall 10 minutes after the hall goes dark. Acknowledged writes lost counts confirmed entries the promoted new hall lacks. Record numbers issued twice counts numbers confirmed to two different people. Stale reads counts the new hall's notice board missing an old-hall entry 30 s after it was made. Changing any control replays from 23:57:20. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: as now, run to the end. At 23:59:00 the scans, No. 4471 and No. 4472 were never sent; at 00:04:00 the new hall is promoted lacking all 3; by morning 4471, 4472 and 4473 are each issued twice, with 3 stale reads. Turn fencing on: still 3 lost, 2 issued twice, and the 05:52 birth crosses the bridge. With fencing off, move the dark to 23:58:00: only the scans are lost, the couple become the new hall's No. 4471, and the old hall gives 4471 out again at 05:52. Back to 23:59:00 with fencing on, and pick semi-sync to one: the couple wait for a copy, are never confirmed, and are married at the new hall at 00:09:00 as No. 4471; nothing lost, nothing issued twice. Pick sync to all: before the night, certificates already wait 2.2 s / 6.3 s, and by morning 8 people are turned away. Back to async with manual failover: 5 turned away, nothing lost. Turn fencing off, pick automatic after 10 s and the 43 s line drop: the new hall is promoted at 23:59:10 while the old hall stays lit, and both halls register all night; fencing on leaves one register, but still 3 lost. Last, no failure with semi-sync: No. 4471's certificate takes 78.2 s, and the new hall's lag p99 is 122.2 s while its p50 stays 2.2 s.

explain.oneLine: Nothing married the couple in one world and not the other. The old hall confirmed No. 4471 the moment it wrote it, while the entry was still queued on its line behind 600 pages of scans; then the old hall went dark, and the watchdog made a copy that had never received it the register, numbering from where its book stopped.

steps.title: One leader, two followers, one log.
steps.text: The old hall is the leader: every registration is written there first, into its log. That's the write-ahead log of the ship's engine room, where each change is recorded before it's made. The annex and the new hall are followers: each receives the leader's log and replays it in the same order, so its book ends up the same, only later. Followers can answer reads, as the copies in the library's back room did, but they never take a write of their own. This copying, called replication, works in steps. First the leader writes an entry into its log. Next it sends the log down the line, one entry after another; if the line is busy or cut, entries wait. Then each follower receives the entries and replays them in order; while entries wait, the follower falls behind. The order is what made Saturday go wrong. No entry can overtake the one in front of it. At 23:57:30 Absalom's 600 pages of scans went into the log, and the line out was busy with them for 120 s, until 23:59:30. The marriage at 23:58:12 and the birth at 23:58:41 queued behind them, unsent, while the counter printed their certificates.

steps.title: When does the leader say done?
steps.text: That moment is the replication mode. Asynchronous, as the halls ran: the leader confirms as soon as its own log has the entry, so a certificate takes 0.0 s, and for a while the entry exists nowhere else. Synchronous: the leader confirms only when every follower it names has the entry. PostgreSQL calls the leader the primary and a follower a standby. Its manual says the minimum wait is the round-trip time between primary and standby: the time for a message to go there and an answer to come back. With every follower required, each certificate waits for the slowest one, the new hall: 2.2 s at p50 and 6.3 s at p99. Semi-synchronous sits between: wait for at least one follower. MySQL, another widely used database, describes its semisynchronous replication exactly so in its manual, and says it works best for close servers communicating over fast networks; the annex answers in 0.2 s at p50 and 0.4 s at p99. In PostgreSQL, a commit with standbys works in steps. The primary writes the commit to its own log. It sends it to the standbys named in synchronous_standby_names: FIRST 2 (s1, s2) waits for both, ANY 1 (s1, s2) for whichever answers first. When enough have saved it, the commit is confirmed. A second setting, synchronous_commit, decides whether a commit waits for them at all; it can even differ from one transaction, one group of changes, to the next. The cost isn't only time. Such commits may never be completed if any one of the synchronous standbys should crash, the manual warns: with every follower required, one dead follower stops every write.

steps.title: Lag is a distribution, and the tail is where you lose.
steps.text: Mr Threlfall's seconds behind was true at the median, the middle value: over the hour before, half the entries reached the new hall within 2.2 s and 99 in 100 within 6.3 s. But the number that decides a failover is the lag at the moment of failure, and that sits in the tail, the slowest few entries. A large write makes the tail: everything behind the scans waited, so the new hall was 42 s behind at 23:58:12 and 90 s behind at 23:59:00. On a night with no failure the sim shows the same thing plainly: the new hall's p50 stays 2.2 s while its p99 jumps to 122.2 s. The library case had a fix called read-your-writes: so you always see your own change, your reads go to the leader for a few seconds after you write. That window only works while the lag stays under it. A failover breaks your own writes in a worse way: the write isn't late, it's gone.

steps.title: Failover loses what never arrived.
steps.text: A failover works in steps. First the watchdog notices silence, here for five minutes. Then it promotes a follower: the follower stops replaying the log and starts taking writes. From then on it numbers new entries from where its own book stopped. What can go wrong is what the follower never received. At 00:04:00 the watchdog promoted the new hall, and the new hall could only become the register it had. It lacked the scans, No. 4471 and No. 4472, all three confirmed: 3 acknowledged writes lost. PostgreSQL's manual says it plainly: if the primary crashes, some transactions that were committed may not have been replicated to the standby, and the amount of data loss is proportional to the replication delay at the time of failover. How much confirmed work you accept losing is your RPO, short for recovery point objective. With an async follower it's roughly the lag's tail. Promoting faster doesn't shrink it: at 10 s the same 3 entries are lost, because they never left the old hall. Waiting for one follower does. With semi-sync the marriage was never confirmed, so nobody was promised it, and the couple registered again at 00:09:00. That holds only if the failover uses what the confirming follower has, here by copying from the annex before promoting.

steps.title: The old leader comes back.
steps.text: At 05:47 the old hall came back still believing it was the register, and at 05:52 it gave out No. 4473 again. Two copies each taking writes as leader is split brain, and their books diverge, drifting apart: 4471, 4472 and 4473 now belong to two people each. Fencing prevents it. It works in steps. First, before promoting anyone, the watchdog reaches the old leader by some other route. Then it makes sure the old leader can't take writes any more, by cutting its power, taking away its access or, as here, locking its register so it comes back read-only. Only then does it promote the follower. If it can't reach the old leader, fencing fails, and promoting anyway risks two leaders. With fencing, the 05:52 birth crossed the bridge and got the next number in the one register. Fencing can't merge what the old leader holds and nobody else does. The scans, and on Saturday the marriage and the birth, existed only in the old hall's book, and only a person can tell whether two entries are one marriage or two. GitHub, after its own failover in 2018, called this manual reconciliation.

diagram.aria: The fix on next Saturday's night. At 23:58:12 the couple register at the old hall as No. 4471. The line out is busy with the scans, so the entry waits for a copy and no certificate prints. At 23:59:00 the old hall goes dark with No. 4471 never confirmed. At 00:04:00 the watchdog fences the old hall and promotes the new hall. At 00:09:00 the couple register at the new hall, which sends No. 4471 to the annex; the annex has it 2.2 s later and the certificate prints. At 05:47 the old hall comes back read-only and its unconfirmed entries are reconciled by hand. One book, one No. 4471.

explain.caption: Next Saturday with the fix. The old hall prints no certificate until one copy has the entry, so No. 4471 waits behind the scans and is never confirmed before the dark. The watchdog fences the old hall before promoting the new hall, the couple register again at 00:09:00 with a certificate after 2.2 s, and the old hall's unconfirmed entries are reconciled by hand when it comes back read-only.

fix.title: The fix: confirm only what a nearby copy has, fence before promoting, reconcile by hand
fix.text: Make the old hall print a certificate only when one copy has the entry: semi-sync to one follower, which is always the annex, 0.2 s away at p50 and 0.4 s at p99. In PostgreSQL that's synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (annex, westerby)' with synchronous_commit on; in MySQL, semisynchronous replication. Before the watchdog promotes the new hall, it fences the old hall, so the old hall comes back read-only, and copies anything the new hall lacks from the annex. When the old hall comes back, a person compares its unconfirmed entries with the register and reconciles them by hand. On Saturday's replay that means nothing acknowledged lost, no number issued twice and nobody turned away: the couple waited for a certificate that never printed, crossed the bridge and were married at the new hall at 00:09:00 as No. 4471. Then move big jobs like the scans off the register's line at night, or split them, because a big write still makes everyone behind it wait.

limits: Semi-sync only promises that a confirmed entry is on one follower. It helps only if the failover uses that follower, by copying from it first or by promoting it. A watchdog that promotes a copy lacking the entry, without catching up first, loses it all the same.

If no follower answers, the leader has to choose. MySQL's semisynchronous replication reverts to asynchronous after a timeout, a set time with no answer, and goes back to semi-sync when a replica, MySQL's word for a follower, catches up. PostgreSQL waits, and commits stall. Either way, alert when the follower you count on stops answering.

Semi-sync turns a loss into a wait, not into nothing: on a night with no failure, No. 4471's certificate took 78.2 s behind the scans. Large writes still need splitting, or keeping off the line at busy times.

head: Choice
Good
Bad
rows: Certificates at once, 0.0 s. The leader never waits for a copy.
Saturday: 3 confirmed entries lost in the failover, and 4471, 4472 and 4473 issued twice.
Semi-sync to one copy, the annex
Every confirmed entry is in two books. Normally 0.2 s at p50, 0.4 s at p99, and one copy can be down.
Waits behind big writes: 78.2 s for No. 4471 on a night with no failure. The failover must use the annex's book. MySQL can quietly fall back to async.
Every copy has every confirmed entry.
Every certificate waits for the slowest copy, 2.2 s at p50 and 6.3 s at p99. One dark hall stopped every registration: 8 turned away.
The same 3 entries lost. A 43 s line drop makes two registers all night: 4471 to 4473 issued twice.
Manual: wait for the old hall
Nothing lost and never two registers.
No register from 23:59 to 05:47, and 5 people turned away.
One register when the old hall returns: 2 numbers issued twice on Saturday instead of 3, and one register in the line drop.
Brings back nothing that was lost, and needs a way to reach the old hall that the failure didn't cut.

explain.seniorTake: Replication is a promise about when done is true, and a failover is when the promise is collected. Decide for each kind of data how much confirmed work you can lose. Write it down as an RPO, the most you accept losing. Then pick the mode that keeps it. Use async when a few seconds of loss is acceptable. Use semi-sync to a nearby follower when a confirmed write must exist twice. Use sync to all rarely, because it hands every write to your slowest, least reachable copy. Measure lag as a spread, p50 and p99, not one number, and watch its tail, especially during large writes. Make the failover use the most complete follower, fence the old leader before promoting, and plan the reconciliation, because a leader that dies with unsent writes comes back with them. A faster failover shortens the outage; it never brings back a write.

realWorld.title: GitHub, 21 October 2018: 43 seconds
realWorld.text: GitHub's October 21 post-incident analysis begins: at 22:52 UTC on October 21, routine maintenance work to replace failing 100G optical equipment resulted in the loss of connectivity between our US East Coast network hub and our primary US East Coast data center. Connectivity between these locations was restored in 43 seconds, but this brief outage triggered a chain of events that led to 24 hours and 11 minutes of service degradation. GitHub uses Orchestrator, a tool that decides which database copy leads, to manage its MySQL cluster topologies and handle automated failover. In those seconds, the analysis says, the US West Coast data center and US East Coast public cloud Orchestrator nodes were able to establish a quorum, enough of them agreeing to decide, and start failing over clusters to direct writes to the US West Coast data center: a cross-country promotion, triggered by a blip.

realWorld.title: GitHub: two books
realWorld.text: The analysis says the database servers in the US East Coast data center contained a brief period of writes that had not been replicated to the US West Coast facility, while the West Coast database cluster had ingested writes from our application tier for nearly 40 minutes. Each side held writes the other lacked, like the two halls' books, and GitHub writes that it was unable to fail the primary back over to the US East Coast data center safely. With the leaders in the West, GitHub wrote, applications running in the East Coast that depend on writing information to a West Coast MySQL cluster are currently unable to cope with the additional latency introduced by a cross-country round trip for the majority of their database calls.

realWorld.title: GitHub: integrity first, then reconcile
realWorld.text: GitHub chose its order plainly: our strategy was to prioritize data integrity over site usability and time to recovery. The incident resulted in degraded service for 24 hours and 11 minutes. And the unreplicated East Coast writes went to people: ultimately, no user data was lost; however manual reconciliation for a few seconds of database writes is still in progress. GitHub says it was analysing those logs to determine which writes could be reconciled automatically and which would require outreach to users.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL 18: synchronous replication
realWorld.text: PostgreSQL streaming replication, sending the log to standbys as it is written, is asynchronous by default, the manual says, and if the primary server crashes then some transactions that were committed may not have been replicated to the standby server, causing data loss, the amount proportional to the replication delay at the time of failover. Synchronous replication instead makes each commit wait until the commit has been written to the write-ahead log on disk of both the primary and standby server, and then the only possibility that data can be lost is if both the primary and the standby suffer crashes at the same time. The minimum wait time is the round-trip time between primary and standby. synchronous_standby_names takes FIRST, a priority list such as FIRST 2 (s1, s2, s3), or ANY, a quorum such as ANY 2 (s1, s2, s3). Its warning: such transaction commits may never be completed if any one of the synchronous standbys should crash, so name several potential standbys, or lower the number a commit waits for.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL 18: synchronous_commit
realWorld.text: synchronous_commit specifies how much WAL processing must complete before the database server returns a success indication to the client, and is on by default. When synchronous_standby_names is non-empty and it is on, commits wait until replies from the current synchronous standby(s) indicate they have received the commit record of the transaction and flushed it to durable storage. It can be changed at any time, and the manual calls it possible, and useful, to have some transactions commit synchronously and others asynchronously. A town could wait for a copy on a marriage and not on a page of scans.

realWorld.title: MySQL 8.4: semisynchronous replication
realWorld.text: MySQL's manual says that with asynchronous replication, if the source crashes, transactions that it has committed might not have been transmitted to any replica, and failover might result in failover to a server that is missing transactions relative to the source. Semisynchronous replication falls between asynchronous and fully synchronous replication: the source waits until at least one replica has received and logged the events, and the replica acknowledges only after the events have been written to its relay log, its file of received changes, and flushed to disk. The slowdown is at least the TCP/IP roundtrip time, one trip over the network and back, so it works best for close servers communicating over fast networks. If a timeout occurs without any replica having acknowledged the transaction, the source reverts to asynchronous replication. Fully synchronous replication means failover to any replica is possible at any time, with the drawback that there might be a lot of delay to complete a transaction.

realWorld.title: Amazon RDS: a synchronous standby in another zone
realWorld.text: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, AWS says, Amazon RDS, Amazon's rented-database service, automatically provisions and maintains a synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone, a separate building with its own power. The price is written down too: such instances can have increased write and commit latency compared to a Single-AZ deployment, because of the synchronous data replication that occurs. And the standby is for failover only: you can't use a standby replica to serve read traffic.

asked: Synchronous or asynchronous replication: what's the difference, and which would you choose?
What can you lose in a failover, and how do you limit it?
interview.answer: In leader-follower replication the leader takes every write and followers replay its log in order. The difference is when the leader tells the client, the program that sent the write, that it's done. Asynchronous: as soon as its own log has it. Writes are fast, but a follower is always a little behind, usually under a second or two, much more during large writes. A failover to it loses every confirmed write it hadn't received. That loss is your RPO, the recovery point objective. It's set by the lag's tail at the moment of failure, not its median, so measure lag as p50 and p99. Synchronous to every follower loses nothing on failover, but every write waits for the slowest follower, and if one dies, writes stop: PostgreSQL warns such commits may never be completed. The usual middle is semi-synchronous, or in PostgreSQL ANY 1 over a list of standbys: wait for one nearby follower, so a confirmed write exists twice for the cost of a short round trip, and keep distant followers async for disasters. Then make failover use the most complete follower, and alert when the follower you count on stops answering, since MySQL quietly falls back to async after a timeout. Split brain is two nodes, two database machines, both acting as leader and taking writes, usually because a follower was promoted while the old leader was alive behind a network blip, or because the old leader came back. The books diverge and IDs collide. Prevent it with fencing: before promoting, make sure the old leader can't accept writes, by cutting its power or access or forcing it read-only. Whatever it holds that the new leader doesn't must be reconciled, often by hand. GitHub's October 2018 incident is the classic example: 43 seconds of lost connectivity, a cross-country promotion, writes on both coasts, and 24 hours and 11 minutes of degraded service.

terms.def: A town's official book of births, deaths and marriages. Each entry gets the next record number, and the person gets a certificate.
The Osterby custom of keeping the register open all night, so people can register at any hour.
The number a register gives each entry: one more than its last. Each hall numbers from its own book, which is how both gave out 4471.
The paper a hall prints when it has registered an entry. In this case, printing it is the leader acknowledging the write.
A records room across the square from the old hall that keeps a copy of the register: a follower 0.2 s behind at p50. It has no counter.
The old hall's one line for its log. It sends entries one at a time, in order, to both copies. On Saturday the scans held it for 120 s.
600 scanned pages of the 1911 register that Absalom filed at 23:57:30. One large write: the line out needed 120 s to send it.
Mr Threlfall's program in the new hall. When the old hall has been silent for a set time, it promotes the new hall to be the register.
The new hall's public list of new entries. It reads each old-hall entry from the new hall's own copy 30 s after it is made.
The one copy of a database that takes every write and sends its log to the others. Also called the primary or, in MySQL, the source.
A copy that receives the leader's log and replays it in the same order. Also called a replica or a standby. It takes no writes of its own.
One leader takes every write, and followers replay its log to keep copies. Also called primary-replica or single-leader replication.
When the leader tells the client a write is done: at once (async), when one follower has it (semi-sync), or when every named follower has it (sync).
Semi-sync for short. The leader confirms a write once at least one follower has received it, not all of them. MySQL calls it semisynchronous replication.
The sim's name for making every write wait until every other copy has it. The safest against loss, and stopped by any one copy that is down.
A write the leader has told the client is done. Here, an entry whose certificate has been printed. Also called a confirmed write.
An entry the leader wrote but never acknowledged, because it was still waiting for a copy when the leader died or was fenced.
The 50th percentile, or median: half the measurements are at or below it. The new hall's lag over the hour was p50 2.2 s.
Replication lag described by its spread, not one number: p50 for the usual case, p99 for the tail, which large writes make longer.
One change so big that sending it holds the log line for a while, like the 600 pages of scans. Every entry behind it waits.
A program promotes a follower when the leader has been silent for a set time, with no person deciding. The watchdog is one.
A person decides whether and when to promote a follower. In the sim, the registrar waits for the old hall instead.
Making sure an old leader can't take writes after a failover, even if it wakes up: cutting its power or access, or forcing it read-only.
Two copies each acting as the leader and taking writes at once, so their data diverges. Usually from a promotion during a network blip.
Two copies each holding writes the other lacks, so neither is the whole truth, like 4471 being a wedding in one book and a death in the other.
A person comparing two copies after divergence and deciding entry by entry what to keep, merge, renumber or re-enter.
Recovery point objective: how much recently confirmed data you accept losing in a failure, stated as time, such as at most 5 seconds of writes.
A read from a follower that hasn't received a write the leader already has, so it answers with older data or none.
The sim's count of registrations no register could take: no register at all, or one that can't get the copies its mode needs.
The sim's count of record numbers confirmed to two different people, one in each hall's book.
A PostgreSQL setting naming the standbys a commit waits for. FIRST 2 (s1, s2) waits for the first two by priority; ANY 1 (s1, s2) for any one.
The two forms of synchronous_standby_names. FIRST picks standbys by their order in the list; ANY waits for any that many, a quorum.
When synchronous_standby_names is set, synchronous_commit on makes each commit wait until the named standbys have saved it to disk.
Enough members of a group agreeing for a decision to count, such as any 2 of 3 standbys. The next case uses it for reads and writes.
A MySQL replica's file of the events it has received from the source, before it applies them. Semi-sync acknowledges once they are in it.
MySQL's words for one message over the network and its answer back. TCP/IP is the set of rules the internet sends data by. It is the least a semi-sync commit adds to each write.
A free tool that keeps track of which MySQL copy leads and which follow, and runs failovers automatically. GitHub used it in 2018.
Which copy is the leader and which follow it, and from where. A failover changes the topology.
A message sent across the United States and back, tens of milliseconds, instead of within one data center, well under one.
A company's written account of an outage after it is over: what happened, why, and what will change. GitHub published one for October 2018.
An Amazon RDS database with a synchronous standby in a different availability zone, a separate building with its own power, kept for failover. The standby can't answer reads.
A rule in ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a security standard companies are audited against: keep enough spare machines and copies that systems stay available when one fails.
An optional part of a SOC 2 report, an auditor's report on a company's controls. The AICPA, the US accountants' body, defines it as systems being available for use to meet the company's objectives.
The Build Night project that simulates a system from a file describing its parts. Its L4 night adds the data tier, the databases: copies, lag and shards (a database split into pieces).

atWork: Picture a common incident: a team's managed database, one a cloud company runs for them, fails over in the night, the dashboard shows a minute of downtime, and next morning support finds the last minute of orders missing, confirmed to customers by email but nowhere in the database. The replica that was promoted was asynchronous, and those orders never reached it. Look for the same in your own systems. With read-only access, find out how each database you own replicates. In PostgreSQL, the command SHOW prints a setting: run SHOW synchronous_standby_names; and SHOW synchronous_commit;. On Amazon RDS, Amazon's rented-database service, check whether it is a Multi-AZ DB instance, whose standby AWS describes as synchronous, or relies on read replicas, which are asynchronous. Then write the RPO down in plain words, such as a failover loses at most the writes of the last 5 seconds, and compare it with the replica lag's p99, not its average. Test it in steps, on a staging copy, a practice copy no customer uses. Write numbered rows without stopping. Stop the primary, the leader. Let the failover run. Count which numbers are missing. Then do it again during a big batch write, one large write of many rows at once, and ask what happens to the old primary when it comes back. This rehearses the L4 Build Night in Loadout, the data tier: model replication lag as a spread with a p50, a p99 and spikes during large writes, count stale reads, and record in docs/decisions.md, the project's decisions file, what your lag model says about read-your-writes. If your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a security standard companies are audited against, control A.8.14 (redundancy of information processing facilities) expects enough redundancy to meet availability requirements, and a stated RPO, a tested failover and its results are the kind of evidence an auditor looks for. If it is pursuing a SOC 2 report, an auditor's report on its controls, that includes the availability category, criterion A1.3 expects the entity to test recovery plan procedures, so build the failover test in from the start rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: A shop's PostgreSQL primary, its leader, streams its log to one standby, a follower kept ready to take over, in another region, asynchronously. Last night the primary's zone failed, and the standby was promoted automatically 20 seconds later. This morning 14 customers have order confirmation emails for orders the database doesn't have. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The orders were confirmed before the standby had them, and promoting a standby that never received them lost them
Make each commit wait for one nearby follower (semi-sync, or synchronous_standby_names with ANY 1), so a confirmed order always exists twice
Fence the old primary and recover the missing orders by hand, from its disk or the emails, then reconcile

recall.model: The shop confirmed each order the moment the primary committed it, before the standby had it: asynchronous replication. The standby was behind, as async standbys usually are, and when it was promoted every order that had never reached it was gone, though the customers had their emails. A faster or slower failover wouldn't have changed that. Make each commit wait for one follower: add a standby in the same region, list it with synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (...)' and keep synchronous_commit on, so a confirmed order always exists in two places for the cost of one short round trip, and keep the far standby async for disasters. Make the failover promote, or first copy from, the standby that has everything. Fence the old primary so it can't come back taking orders, and recover the 14 orders by hand, from the old primary's disk if it can be read, otherwise from the emails, then reconcile them into the new primary.

recall.prompt: Your team runs PostgreSQL with two standbys and synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 2 (s1, s2)', so every commit waits for both. During a network fault, s2 can't be reached for 4 minutes. What happens to writes, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Commits wait for s2 and may never complete while it is unreachable: writes stop for the whole fault
Wait for any one of the two instead (ANY 1 or FIRST 1), or name more candidate standbys
The cost: every commit already waits for the slower standby's round trip, so keep the one that answers close

recall.model: With FIRST 2, every commit waits until both standbys have it, so while s2 can't be reached, commits wait for it: PostgreSQL warns such commits may never be completed if any one of the synchronous standbys should crash. Four minutes of no writes. Change it to wait for any one of the two, synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (s1, s2)': a confirmed commit still exists on at least one standby, and losing either no longer stops writes. Each commit waits a round trip to the first standby that answers, and with FIRST 2 every commit was already as slow as the slower standby, so keep at least one standby close by. Then alert when fewer standbys than you need are connected.

recall.prompt: In GitHub's 21 October 2018 incident, what did its post-incident analysis say the US East Coast database servers held after the failover?
options: Nothing new: every write had reached the West Coast before the 43 s ended
Corrupted pages, because the network cut interrupted writes halfway through
A brief period of writes that had not been replicated to the West Coast
Copies of the West Coast's new writes, sent back over the restored link
recall.why: GitHub writes: the database servers in the US East Coast data center contained a brief period of writes that had not been replicated to the US West Coast facility. Meanwhile the West Coast cluster had taken writes from the application tier for nearly 40 minutes, so each side held writes the other lacked, and GitHub says it was unable to fail the primary back over to the East Coast safely. It reported that no user data was lost, with manual reconciliation for a few seconds of database writes still in progress.

recall.prompt: After a failover, the old leader comes back, still believes it is the leader, and takes writes while the new leader does too. What is this called, and what prevents it?
options: Split brain; fence the old leader so it can't take writes before promoting
Lag spike; add a faster line so the follower catches up sooner
A stale read; send every read to the new leader for a few seconds
Leader drift; make the watchdog wait longer before it promotes the copy
recall.why: Two copies taking writes as leader at once is split brain, and their data diverges, as 4471 to 4473 did at the halls. Fencing prevents it: before the new leader is promoted, make sure the old one can't accept writes, by cutting its power or access or forcing it read-only. A faster line, reading from the leader or a longer wait don't stop a returning leader from taking writes.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The old hall waits for one copy before printing a certificate, the watchdog fences it before promoting, and Absalom files scans in the afternoon. Last month Mr Threlfall moved the register to MySQL, with semisynchronous replication to the annex only: the old hall waits for the annex alone. The new hall gets the log the ordinary way, without being waited for. On Tuesday at 21:10 a digger cut the annex's line. The old hall kept printing certificates. At 23:40 it went dark, the watchdog fenced it and promoted us, and two births registered in the last two seconds before the dark were in neither copy. Both families have certificates. Mr Threlfall says it can't be: semi-sync can't lose a certificate.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. How did a semi-sync register lose two certificates, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: With no copy acknowledging, MySQL reverted to asynchronous replication after a timeout, so certificates went out with no copy holding them
Alert when semi-sync is off or no copy is acknowledging, so a person knows the promise has lapsed
Let either copy acknowledge, so one cut line doesn't remove the guarantee
match: the annex or the new hall

coldCase.model: Semi-sync only promises that a copy has the entry while a copy is answering. MySQL's source waits for an acknowledgement, and if a timeout occurs without any replica acknowledging, it reverts to asynchronous replication, quietly, until a replica catches up. From 21:10 every certificate was async again, and the two births in the last seconds before 23:40 had reached neither copy: the new hall was its usual couple of seconds behind. Change three things. Let either copy acknowledge, the annex or the new hall, so one cut line doesn't remove the guarantee. Alert the moment semi-sync is off or no copy is acknowledging, so a person decides whether to keep printing. And reconcile the two births by hand from the old hall's book once it can be read.

next: Next, Two Leaders: a commune with two councils, and databases where more than one copy takes writes, with their conflicts and quorums.

PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, 19.5 Write Ahead Log (synchronous_commit: on by default; with synchronous_standby_names set, commits wait for the synchronous standbys to flush the commit record; can differ per transaction)

Linford & Co: Availability Trust Services Criteria in a SOC 2 Audit (quotes the AICPA: information and systems are available for operation and use to meet the entity's objectives; A1.3, the entity tests recovery plan procedures supporting system recovery to meet its objectives)
